sentences: Artificial intelligence developer OpenAI has established a major partnership with the United States Department of Defense (DoD) to deploy its technology on classified military networks.

The San Francisco-based firm announced this week that it would make its Daybreak cybersecurity AI models available for use by the members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) military alliance.
The specialized program was designed for vetted, authorized cybersecurity defenders, and it will be used by NATO’s Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) to protect alliance networks.

According to OpenAI, NATO has already used approximately 300 billion raw input and output tokens monthly. (In plain English, a token is the most basic unit of data —which could include a word, part of a word, or even a punctuation mark—that an AI model reads, processes, and generates.

Unlike humans, who typically read text as full sentences, AI utilizes a “tokenizer” that breaks down text into smaller chunks, which are then processed accordingly.)
OpenAI’s Daybreak will aid NATO in examining code, scanning for odd network behavior, and confirming weaknesses.
It can then build and trial patches.
“AI-powered cyber defence models represent a generational leap in cyber security,” said Dr.
Dylan Browne, the NCIA’s general manager.
Browne claimed that the models could accelerate vulnerability discovery and help detect emerging threats at machine speed, which could enable defenders to stay ahead of potential adversaries.

“For NATO, these technologies strengthen our cyber resilience, enhance our operational advantage and reinforce our ability to protect critical digital infrastructure at unprecedented scale and speed,” Browne said.
“As we scale adoption, we will build a deeper understanding of token consumption, usage patterns and the underlying economics of AI models.

This insight will help us optimize costs, evaluate competing solutions and make informed procurement decisions.”
OpenAI and NATO continue to use the term “artificial intelligence,” even as US President Donald Trump has directed all federal departments and agencies to use the term “super intelligence” (SI) in official correspondence, public communications, websites, and policy documents.

Earlier this year, OpenAI supported NATO’s Crossed Swords 2026, the alliance’s annual, full-spectrum cyber operations and multi-domain military exercise organized by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE).

The exercise, which took place in Tallinn, Estonia, earlier this month, saw around 250 participants from more than 40 NATO and non-NATO partner countries—including military cyber operators, threat hunters, digital forensics specialists, and special operations units—take part in offensive and defensive cyberspace operations.

Part of this year’s cyber drills saw participants build, deploy, and assess AI agents for cyber operations, utilizing local environments and OpenAI’s Daybreak cyber defense offering under human oversight.
It marked the first time the platform was employed in such an exercise.
The emphasis remains on maintaining human oversight of the AI models.
“The people defending our democracies should have the most advanced technology on their side.
NATO’s cyber defenders protect networks that are essential to the security of the Alliance.

Through Daybreak, we’re putting more capable tools in their hands to help them find and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them,” said Sasha Baker, head of national security policy at OpenAI.

“We look forward to deepening this work with NATO and our allies, helping turn advances in AI into stronger cyber defenses.”
The adoption of OpenAI’s Daybreak AI cybersecurity initiative is just one aspect of NATO’s continued embrace of emerging technologies to help the alliance protect against rising threats.

At the 2025 NATO Summit in The Hague, the allied leaders endorsed NATO’s Rapid Adoption Action Plan, which called for significantly accelerating the pace at which the alliance adopts new technologies and integrates them into Allied armed forces.
“Although many of the technologies that are reshaping the world today are new, the need for innovation is not,” the alliance wrote in a media release.

“Since its founding in 1949, NATO has stayed at the forefront of technology to ensure the defence of its member countries and the success of its operations.”
